the nuclear hard X-ray luminosity of early-type galaxies is not tightly related to the galactic properties, but it shows a large variation at any fixed galactic luminosity or black hole mass, which can be explained by differences in the fuel supply and/or in the effective accretion rate.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the origin of the nuclear X-ray emission in early-type galaxies, and it suggests that the observed wide range of L X,nucleus at fixed LB or M BH reflects the large variety of physical conditions in the nuclear region, and in particular of the fuel availability.

the origin of the observed large scatter in L X,nuc at fixed LB (and M BH) that cannot be explained by the expected dependence of the mass accreting onto the black hole with the galactic structure and gas content.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, while the nuclear emission is not tightly correlated to the fuel availability in the circumnuclear or global galactic scale (as expected in a steady accretion scenario), it can be correlated with the galactic structure (as expected in the case of a quasi-steady accretion with a variable fuel production rate), although this correlation is not tight either, and is present only in a subset of the galaxies.

the nuclear X-ray emission of nearby early-type galaxies is produced by accretion onto a supermassive black hole, and its observed variation is due to the interplay of different processes that are still to be fully understood.

the observed L X,ISM and cuspiness variations are the main causes of the L X,nuc differences in the sample, with a possible contribution of other factors such as the age of the central galactic population and/or a cycle of activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
L X,nuc is linked to both the circumnuclear structure and the total gas content, and that the nuclear emission is likely to be produced in the hot gas.
the observed L X,ISM-L X,nuc correlation is the result of a complex interplay between the hot gas content and the black hole activity, and it is likely related to the feedback process.

the observed large variation of L X, nuc at a given LB or M BH, and the observed trends of L X,n uc with the inner structure and with the galactic hot gas content, are compatible with a scenario where accreting black holes are regulated by the availability of the circumnuclear fuel, and the mass accreted is largely reduced by winds/outflows.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the nuclear X-ray luminosity of early-type galaxies is a complex quantity, which depends on the black hole mass, the galactic structure, the hot gas content and possibly on the age of its stellar component.

, in the absence of a tight relationship with the fuel production rate and the circumnucleus gas content, L X,nuclei is likely determined by the black hole feedback, which regulates the accretion process and the nuclear X-ray emission.

the nuclear hard X-ray luminosity of nearby early-type galaxies is not simply linked to the central galactic structure and gas content, and that the accretion rate on the black hole is likely not a steady process.
